say: You give it a **right-angled** triangle with two sides known. It gives back the third side.
The key idea: the square on the longest side (the hypotenuse) equals the sum of the squares on the other two. Find which side is the longest first.
what.in: two sides of a right angle

how.higher: Higher level uses it as a step inside bigger Paper 2 questions (2023 Question 7, 2022 Question 9) and in a 15-mark Paper 1 problem on travel times (2025 Question 8), usually before a rounding or a unit conversion.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it as a short part of a Paper 2 question (2025 Question 5(b)(i), 2023 Question 5(d), 2021 Question 2(b)), often with a diagram, and always with rounding.

example.question: A ladder $7$ m long leans against a vertical wall. Its foot is $2$ m from the wall. How high up the wall does the ladder reach? Give your answer correct to one decimal place.

steps.title: Find the hypotenuse
steps.say: The wall and the ground meet at a right angle. The ladder is opposite that angle, so it is the longest side. Call the height $\hl{1}{h}$.

lines.text: Hypotenuse $= 7$. The other two sides are $2$ and $\hl{1}{h}$.

steps.title: Write Pythagoras
steps.say: The square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

steps.title: Solve for h
steps.say: Get $\hl{1}{h}^2$ on its own by taking $2^2$ from both sides.

ordinary.tip: Write the formula and substitute into it. No formula and no correct substitution earns nothing.

say: You give it an **angle of elevation** (or depression) and one distance. It gives back a height or a distance.
The key idea: the angle is measured from the **horizontal**. Draw the right-angled triangle, label the sides from that angle, and pick sine, cosine or tangent.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as one step in a longer Paper 2 question (2023 Question 7(b), 2025 Question 8(c)(ii)), often after the sine rule has found a distance first.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asked for it once, in 2022 Paper 2 Question 8(d): an angle of $1.2°$ and one length, tan to find a distance.

example.question: A tree stands on level ground. From a point $45$ m from its base, the angle of elevation of the top of the tree is $28°$. Find the height of the tree, correct to one decimal place.

steps.title: Draw and label
steps.say: Draw the ground, the tree and the line of sight. The angle $28°$ is at your feet. The tree is **opposite** it. The $45$ m is **adjacent** to it.

steps.title: Choose the ratio
steps.say: We have the adjacent and want the opposite. That is tangent.

steps.title: Solve for h
steps.say: Multiply both sides by $45$. Your calculator must be in degree mode.

higher.tip: Set the calculator to degree mode. A wrong mode is a named loss, even if the method is right.
Round at the end to the accuracy asked. Not rounding loses a mark.
Write the trig ratio with the correct sides. Marks are given for the ratio set up correctly.

ordinary.tip: Write the trig formula first. Writing it down earns the first mark on its own.
Round as asked, and show the equation before the answer. A correct value with wrong rounding loses marks.

say: You give it **two sides** and the angle **between** them. It gives back the area of the triangle.
The key idea: the angle must be the included angle, the one the two sides make. Then area $= \frac12 ab\sin C$.

how.higher: Higher level uses it often on Paper 2, as a part of its own or inside a longer question (2025 Question 8(a)(ii), 2024 Question 3(a), 2022 Question 9(a)): fields, or the faces of a solid.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it almost every year on Paper 2, as a short part (2025 Question 10(a)(ii), 2024 Question 8(b)(iii), 2023 Question 10(b)), often followed by adding or doubling areas.

example.question: In triangle $ABC$, $|AB| = 9$ cm, $|AC| = 12$ cm and $|\angle BAC| = 40°$. Find the area of the triangle, correct to one decimal place.

steps.title: Check the angle
steps.say: The angle $40°$ is at $A$, between sides $AB$ and $AC$. It is the included angle, so the formula applies.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.say: Write the formula, then put the numbers in.

steps.title: Calculate
steps.say: Do $\frac12 \times 9 \times 12$ first, then multiply by $\sin 40°$ in degree mode.

Round correctly and keep the calculator in degree mode. Both are named losses.

ordinary.tip: Write the formula fully substituted. It has its own mark.
Round as asked. A star is applied for no or wrong rounding.

ordinary.tip: Show the working. A correct answer with no supporting work does not get full credit.
Put units on the answer. No units costs a star.

say: You give it a triangle where you know an **angle and the side opposite it**, plus one more angle or side. It gives back a missing side or angle.
The key idea: each side divided by the sine of the angle **opposite** it gives the same number. Find the third angle first if you need it.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as a step in longer Paper 2 questions (2025 Question 8(c), 2021 Question 9(a), 2024 Question 3(c)), often to find an angle and then something else.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it nearly every year on Paper 2, as a short part (2025 Question 2(b), 2023 Question 7(b), 2021 Question 9(b)(i)), usually with the third angle to find first.

example.question: In triangle $PQR$, $|\angle P| = 48°$, $|\angle Q| = 65°$ and $|QR| = 14$ cm. Find $|PR|$, correct to one decimal place.

steps.title: Match sides to angles
steps.say: $QR$ is opposite $P$, so we know the pair $48°$ and $14$. We want $\hl{1}{|PR|}$, which is opposite $Q = 65°$.

lines.text: Known pair: $48°$ and $14$. Wanted side is opposite $65°$.

steps.title: Write the sine rule
steps.say: Put the side we want over its angle on one side. Put the known pair on the other.
